title: M/S Dev Prayag Paper Mill (Pvt.) & Ors. v. State of U.P. & Ors. (batch of ~90 connected writ petitions)
coram: Dilip B. Bhosale, Chief Justice & Yashwant Varma, J. (delivered by Bhosale, CJ)
docket: WRIT - C No. 30898 of 2016 (leading case; batch of ~90 connected writ petitions)
disposition: Writ petitions dismissed; all interim orders discharged
headnote: Clause 4.20(l) of the U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (barring a distribution licensee from requiring security under Section 47(1) if the consumer is prepared to take supply through a prepayment meter, 'as and when' the licensee offers that choice) is not ultra vires Section 47(5) of the Electricity Act, 2003. Section 47(5) is not a free-standing override of Section 47(1)-(4); the words 'subject to the provisions of this section' in Section 47(1) mean the security determination is governed by Section 47 read as a whole, not subservient only to sub-section (5). The exemption from security in sub-section (5) is conditioned on the actual availability of a prepayment meter — the consumer's mere 'preparedness' to take supply through such a meter does not, by itself, denude the licensee of the power to demand security where prepayment meters for the relevant consumer category (here, High Tension consumers) are not manufactured or available in the market; a demand for additional security on account of increased consumption remains valid until such meters become available. Read with Section 55 (which only mandates a 'correct meter', not a prepayment meter), Clause 4.20(l) tracks and does not exceed Section 47(5).

holding_units.code: U.P. Electricity Supply Code, 2005 (with s.47(5), EA 2003)
holding_units.topic: Prepayment-meter exemption from security deposit is conditional on availability of the meter; Clause 4.20(l) not ultra vires s.47(5)
holding_units.question: Is Clause 4.20(l) of the Supply Code, 2005 — which withholds the prepayment-meter security exemption until the licensee offers the consumer a choice to opt for such a meter — ultra vires Section 47(5) of the Act, 2003, and can an HT consumer avoid a demand for additional security merely by expressing willingness to take supply through a prepayment meter that is not actually available?
holding_units.holding: No, the clause is intra vires, and no, mere willingness does not suffice. Section 47(5) exempts a consumer from security only where the consumer is 'prepared' to take supply through a prepayment meter, and this preparedness is itself contingent on the actual availability of such a meter; Section 55 separately mandates only a 'correct meter', not a prepayment meter. Since prepayment meters for HT consumption are neither manufactured nor available in the Indian market, the licensee is under no obligation to install one merely on request, and the exemption in Section 47(5) does not arise. Clause 4.20(l) of the Supply Code, which links the exemption to the licensee 'providing a choice to consumer to opt' for a prepaid meter, does no more than track Section 47(5) and is not an independent or additional fetter; it is not ultra vires. Consequently, a demand for additional security on account of increased HT consumption, made while prepayment meters remain unavailable, is valid.
holding_units.limiting_facts: A batch of ~90 writ petitions by High Tension consumers challenged demand notices for additional/revised security deposit issued under Clause 4.20 read with s.47, after the consumers had written to the licensee requesting installation of prepaid meters under s.47(5); it was undisputed that prepayment meters for HT consumers were neither manufactured nor available in the market, and none of the petitioners challenged the quantum of the demand or the validity of security under s.47(1) as such.

holding_units.clause: s.47(1) ('subject to the provisions of this section')
holding_units.topic: 'Subject to the provisions of this section' in s.47(1) means s.47 read as a whole, not subservient to sub-section (5) alone
holding_units.holding: The words 'subject to the provisions of this section' in Section 47(1) indicate that the fixation of reasonable security is governed by Section 47 read as a whole; sub-sections (1) and (2) are not made subject to sub-section (5) alone, rejecting the petitioners' submission (relying on the Black's Law Dictionary meaning of 'subject to' as explained in Saurashtra Chemicals) that sub-section (5) overrides sub-sections (1)-(4).

principle_tags.application: The s.47(5)/Clause 4.20(l) security exemption for consumers willing to take supply through a prepayment meter operates only once such meters are actually available for that consumer category; unavailability (as for HT consumers) leaves the licensee's ordinary power to demand security under s.47(1)-(4) intact. Followed and agreed with the Telangana/AP High Court's parallel ruling in Sarwottam Ispat.

lead_authorities.name: Sarwottam Ispat Ltd. v. Southern Power Distribution Company of Telangana Ltd. & Ors.

not_decided.point: Whether the absence of regulations under Section 181 (as opposed to the Supply Code) renders the demand for security without authority of law
not_decided.note: Not examined in detail — raised only in oral submissions, not pleaded in any of the writ petitions, and in any event the Supply Code was held to cover the field that regulations would otherwise have addressed.

authorities.name: Sarwottam Ispat Ltd. v. Southern Power Distribution Company of Telangana Ltd. & Ors.
authorities.court: High Court of Judicature at Hyderabad (DB)
authorities.proposition: Where pre-paid meters are not installed, it is mandatory for consumers to pay the security deposit demanded; a request for a prepaid meter when none is available does not entitle the consumer to a waiver, and Section 47 does not envisage waiver or an alternative mode of security (e.g. bank guarantee) enforceable by writ.
authorities.how_treated: Followed and agreed with in full (the same Chief Justice had been a member of that Division Bench).

authorities.name: Commissioner of Central Excise, Bhavnagar v. Saurashtra Chemicals Ltd.
authorities.proposition: The expression 'subject to' denotes a limitation — 'governed or affected by', 'provided that' — citing Ashok Leyland Ltd. v. State of T.N. and Black's Law Dictionary.
authorities.how_treated: Relied on by the petitioners for the proposition that s.47(5) overrides s.47(1)-(4); the Court accepted the dictionary meaning but held it supported the opposite conclusion — that s.47(1) is governed by s.47 as a whole, not subservient to s.47(5) alone.

authorities.name: United India Insurance Co. Ltd. v. Lehru & Ors.
authorities.proposition: (Cited alongside Saurashtra Chemicals in support of the petitioners' 'subject to' argument.)
authorities.how_treated: Relied on by the petitioners; rejected along with Saurashtra Chemicals for the same reasons.

authorities.name: Chandra Kumar Shah & Anr. v. The District Judge & Ors.
authorities.proposition: The power to frame regulations/rules cannot be read as a source of authority to enact independent legislation or impose obligations not otherwise envisaged by the parent Act.
authorities.how_treated: Cited by the petitioners in support of a contention (that Clause 4.20 exceeds the s.181 regulation-making power) which the Court declined to examine in detail as it was not pleaded and was raised only in oral submissions.

authorities.name: Bharathidasan University & Anr. v. All-India Council for Technical Education & Ors.
authorities.proposition: (Same proposition as Chandra Kumar Shah — regulation-making power is not a source of independent legislative authority.)
authorities.how_treated: Cited to the same effect; not examined in detail for the same reason.
